extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, and fiction writers (creative-writing students/practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidelines for constructing a dramatic premise, creating three-dimensional characters (including a protagonist's compulsion), and structuring conflict so the story proves its premise. Intended as a checklist and tests writers can apply to plays, novels, and dramatic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story must have a premise — a one-sentence proposition the story proves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The premise should state the beginning (a character with the trait), the middle (collision with opposition), and the end (consequence). Examples given: "Stinginess leads to ruin." (The Miser); "Great love defies even death." (Romeo and Juliet); "Ruthless ambition leads to its own destruction." (Macbeth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every protagonist needs a compulsion — an overriding trait, often negative, with the determination that the trait will prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsions include greed, snobbery, extravagance, rigid honor, etc. The compulsion should be strong enough to drive the character toward ruin or salvation and to shape their choices throughout the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Dimensional Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality character is fully fleshed across three dimensions: physiology, sociology, and psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiology: appearance, health, heredity, age, sex, posture. Sociology: class, occupation, religion, family, race, politics, education. Psychology: morals, ambition, frustration, temperament, IQ, abilities, complexes. Flat characters miss one or more dimensions; fully three-dimensional characters are developed in all three areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfying drama features two characters with opposing flaws bound together such that crisis becomes inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The orchestration of opposing forces (characters whose faults oppose each other) produces meaningful dramatic conflict; the opposition should be structured so that crisis and its consequences are inevitable given the characters' compulsions and traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Clear Premise
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story must articulate a single, testable premise; if the premise is unclear, the work lacks the organizing idea that the plot must prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Events Prove the Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Does every event prove or test the premise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each scene and incident should serve to demonstrate, challenge, or develop the premise rather than exist for unrelated interest or diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Protagonist's Compulsion Strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the protagonist's compulsion strong enough to drive ruin (or salvation)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist's overriding trait must be powerful and determinative enough to force consequential choices and to carry the plot toward the promised outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Worthy Antagonists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents must be credible and sufficiently forceful/opposed to the protagonist's compulsion so that conflict is meaningful and stakes are real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test — Resolution Fulfills the Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the resolution fulfill the premise's promise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story's ending should demonstrate the truth of the premise; the consequence shown at the end must logically follow from the beginning and the character collisions in the middle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Dimensional Test for a Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you describe the character's physical, social, and psychological dimensions for at least three sentences each?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot give three sentences for each of the three dimensions (physiology, sociology, psychology), the character is incomplete. Use this as a practical checklist to detect flatness and to prompt deeper character development.
